content: Orthognathic surgery refers to a variety of elective surgical procedures aimed at correcting facial deformities, malocclusion, and functional disorders of the stomatognathic system. These surgeries are classified as clean-contaminated, meaning that while they are performed under sterile conditions, there is a potential for bacterial contamination due to the nature of the surgical site. The role and optimal regimen of antibiotic prophylaxis in preventing surgical site infections (SSIs) in these patients remain subjects of debate. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of antibiotic prophylaxis in preventing SSIs in individuals undergoing orthognathic surgery. A comprehensive search was conducted in June 2014 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL. Additional searches were performed using Google Scholar, manual searches of relevant journals, conference proceedings, and reference lists of potentially relevant articles. No restrictions were applied regarding language, publication date, or study setting. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different antibiotic prophylaxis regimens or placebo in patients undergoing orthognathic surgery. The primary outcome of interest was the occurrence of SSIs, while secondary outcomes included systemic infections, adverse events, duration of hospital stay, and health-related quality of life. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. Antibiotic regimens were categorized into three groups: preoperative prophylaxis (a single dose administered before surgery), short-term prophylaxis (antibiotics given before or during surgery and/or on the same day of surgery), and long-term prophylaxis (antibiotics administered before or during surgery and continued for more than one day postoperatively). When possible, random-effects meta-analyses were performed using inverse variance methods, and results were reported as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A total of 11 trials were included in the review. Most of these studies had an unclear risk of bias, which led to a downgrading of the quality of evidence. Seven trials provided data for the primary outcome, which was pooled for analysis. The findings suggest that long-term antibiotic prophylaxis likely reduces the risk of SSIs compared to short-term prophylaxis, with a relative reduction in SSI risk ranging from 76% to 26% (472 participants; RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.74; moderate-quality evidence). However, there is uncertainty regarding the effectiveness of short-term prophylaxis compared to a single preoperative dose, as the evidence was of low quality (220 participants; RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.22). None of the included trials reported adverse effects associated with the antibiotics used, nor did they assess other secondary outcomes such as systemic infections, duration of hospital stay, or health-related quality of life. Additionally, there was insufficient evidence to determine whether one specific antibiotic regimen was superior to another. In conclusion, for patients undergoing orthognathic surgery, long-term antibiotic prophylaxis appears to reduce the risk of SSIs compared to short-term prophylaxis. However, there is uncertainty about whether short-term prophylaxis is more effective than a single preoperative dose. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify the optimal antibiotic regimen and to assess other important outcomes.
